title: The Mark of Kri: mapping multiple enemies onto face buttons so animation could stay readable
summary: Sony San Diego's action game used the right stick to assign nearby threats to controller symbols, letting Rau attack several opponents with authored motion while a hand-drawn Polynesian-inspired style kept violence unusually clear.

sourceLabels.manual: The Mark of Kri instruction manual

blocks.text: The right stick paints a threat map

Sweeping the analog stick across nearby enemies assigns them PlayStation face-button symbols. The interface converts a surrounding crowd into a small set of explicit relationships. Instead of repeatedly cycling one lock-on target, the player prepares who each button will address, keeping attention on formation rather than a camera-centered reticle.

Once marked, pressing Cross, Circle, Square or Triangle directs Rau toward the associated enemy. Attack sequences still depend on weapon and timing, but target identity remains stable. This inversion gives the controller a spatial memory: the player remembers which person owns a symbol while watching the group move.

Rau must turn, step and transition convincingly between marked threats. Authored motion sells the idea that one warrior is controlling a melee rather than teleporting among selection boxes. The system is strongest when input queues and animation agree, allowing a planned sequence to flow across several positions without losing readable impact.
Weapons alter the number of relationships

A sword, bow, axe or other tool changes reach, available techniques and how many targets can be managed comfortably. Progression therefore expands not only damage but the complexity of the marked crowd. A weapon suited to broad attacks invites different target assignment from one built around deliberate single strikes.
Kuzo turns scouting into a separate verb

Rau's bird companion can observe areas and mark information before entry. The player gains a higher view while the warrior remains vulnerable, connecting reconnaissance to risk. Enemy placement becomes something planned around before combat, supporting stealth paths and making the eventual symbol map feel like the result of knowledge rather than surprise.

Character shapes, bold color and hand-drawn sequences create an animated-adventure surface inspired by Pacific cultures without pursuing realism. Clear limbs and weapons help multi-target combat read at PS2 resolution. The beauty also contrasts with forceful finishing moves, making violence more striking because it occurs inside imagery that initially appears gentle.
Stealth and melee share level space

Rau can avoid, silently remove or openly confront guards. Marking supports both by clarifying nearby bodies before a plan begins. The game is not a fully systemic stealth simulation, but it allows authored arenas to change tempo. A mistake does not always force a reload; it can transform quiet reconnaissance into controlled crowd combat.

Right-stick dead zones, symbol assignment and animation queues need testing with multiple controller types. Widescreen patches can alter which enemies enter the marking field or how off-screen threats are framed. Higher frame rates may disrupt chained transitions. QA should include Kuzo scouting, every weapon and dense encounters where symbol stability matters most.

The Mark of Kri solves a common action problem by admitting that the player cannot watch every opponent equally. It labels a manageable group, binds those labels to familiar buttons and lets animation express the resulting plan. The system feels direct because interface and character motion share responsibility, turning controller layout into a readable model of surrounding danger.
